title.en: Kobo Daishi, the Wonder-Working Saint

region.en: Mount Koya, where the saint's miracles centre
region.zh: 高野山

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The life-cycle of Japan's greatest Buddhist saint: a miraculous birth amid shining light, marvels of calligraphy and magic in China, a return home capped by miracles over water, dead and barren mountain, and a compact with the fox-god Inari; even after burial at Koya he rises from his grave to conduct a dead emperor's funeral rites.
summary.zh: 弘法大師（空海）傳說一生：降生放光、赴唐習法顯神通、歸國後令荒山開花、與稻荷神結盟，死後猶自墳中起而主持天皇葬儀。

sensitivity.note: Hagiographic saint legend of Kobu Daishi (Kukai), founder of Shingon Buddhism, still venerated in living Japanese Buddhism; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The most holy and famous of Japan's Buddhist saints was born in the Baron's Hall by the shore of Byobu in the year 774. At his birth a bright light shone, and the child came into the world with his hands folded as if in prayer. At five years old he sat among the lotuses and conversed with Buddhas, keeping secret the wisdom he gained. On Mount Shashin he tried to sacrifice his own life as an act of propitiation, but angels prevented him until he had fulfilled his destiny. Once, playing at building a clay pagoda, he was surrounded at once by the Four Heavenly Kings; the Imperial Messenger who passed by declared the boy 'a divine prodigy.' At Muroto in Tosa, while he performed his devotions, a bright star fell from heaven into his mouth, and at midnight an evil dragon came against him, but he spat upon it and killed it with his saliva.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In his nineteenth year he took the black robes of a priest. Reading an abstruse book of Shingon doctrine he could not master, he asked and received the Emperor's leave to visit China, where he unravelled its mysteries and attained miraculous saintship. The Chinese Emperor, hearing his fame, bade him rewrite the faded name of a palace room; he did it with a brush in each hand, another in his mouth and two between his toes, earning the name Gohitsu-Osho, 'the Priest who writes with Five Brushes.' Once he flung his brush into the air above a palace gate and the brush made the missing dot and returned to his hand. Leaving China, he threw his thunder-bolt vajra across the ocean waves, and it was afterwards found hanging on a pine at Takano in Japan. On the Naked Mountain he offered incantations so powerful that the barren slopes broke into flowers and trees. He made brackish water pure, raised the dead, and on Mount Fushime the rice-god Inari appeared and accepted his sacrifice; 'Together, you and I,' said Kobo Daishi, 'we will protect this people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The saint died in 834 and was buried in the graveyard of Okunoin at Koya, and lay and priestly mourners wept there. But his miracles did not cease: when Emperor Saga died, his coffin was mysteriously borne through the air to Koya, and Kobo Daishi himself came forth from his grave to perform the funeral obsequies. Emperor Uda received the sacred baptism from him, and when the Imperial Messenger to his temple could not see the saint's face, Kobo guided the worshipper's hand until it touched the saint's knee — a touch the Messenger never forgot. At Kawasaki a temple stands over an image of the saint which he carved of himself while in China and committed to the waves; a fisherman's net caught it, and the trees in the temple grounds, trained like junks under sail, attest the devotion of seafaring folk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Nichiren and the Sword that Broke

region.en: Beach of Koshigoye, Kamakura
region.zh: 鎌倉小町濱處刑地

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The iconoclast founder of the Nichiren sect, who foretold the Mongol invasion and attacked the other Buddhist sects, is sent to be beheaded at Kamakura; his executioner's sword shatters against his praying neck, lightning strikes the shogun's palace, and a rider with a pardon meets the reprieve-messenger at the ford still called the Place of Meeting.
summary.zh: 日蓮預言蒙古入侵、攻擊諸宗，被判斬首。臨刑念佛，劍觸頸即斷，閃電擊中鎌倉宮殿，天光護體；赦使與劊子手使者於今猶稱「相逢川」之渡口相遇。

sensitivity.note: Hagiographic legend of Nichiren (1222–1282), founder of a living Buddhist school; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Nichiren, whose name means Sun Lotus and who was so named because his mother dreamt the sun rested on a lotus when she conceived him, was an iconoclast. Seeing earthquake, hurricane, pestilence and famine ravage Japan, he read in them the hand of Fate rebelling against corrupt religion and politics. The priests had neglected Shaka Muni, the Buddha himself, to worship Amida and Kwannon instead; no one can serve two masters, he cried — no man has two fathers, no sky holds two suns, no country two kings. He sought to replace the mantra Namu Amida Butsu with Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, 'Oh, the Scripture of the Lotus of the Wonderful Law!', and in his Rissho An-Koku Ron he predicted the Mongol invasion and flung bitter attacks at the rival sects.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hojo Tokiyori exiled him to Ito; he escaped and renewed his attacks, and the Regent Tokimune condemned him to be beheaded on the beach of Koshigoye. As he waited for the stroke, Nichiren prayed to Buddha, and the sword broke as it touched his neck. Immediately a flash of lightning struck the palace at Kamakura and a heavenly light surrounded the saint. The awed executioner sent to the Regent for a reprieve, but Tokimune's own horseman bearing a pardon met him at a river now called Yukiai, the Place of Meeting. Nichiren's escape was followed by renewed attacks and a second exile; he took up his abode on Mount Minobu, where a beautiful woman came while he prayed. 'Resume your natural state,' he said; after drinking water she changed into a snake nearly twenty feet long, with iron teeth and golden scales.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Crackling Mountain: Hare and Badger

region.en: An old couple's cottage and a wood-cutting mountain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 老夫婦的山居與伐木山（象徵釘）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A badger freed from his rope kills an old woman, serves her boiled flesh as broth to her husband, and is hunted down by the faithful white hare — burnt on the Crackling Mountain, salted with cayenne, and drowned at last in his clay boat on the way to the moon.
summary.zh: 狸被釋後殺老嫗、煮其肉為湯騙老翁吃下；白兔為主復仇，於喀啦山燒其背、敷辣椒，終以泥舟沉溺之法處死惡狸，忠兔得主人厚待。

sensitivity.note: Japanese animal folktale of the hare-and-badger cycle, with grim anthropophagic imagery; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old man and his wife kept a white hare. One day a badger came and ate the pet's food; the old man caught him and tied him to a tree before leaving to cut wood. The badger wept until the old woman untied the rope, then proclaimed vengeance and ran away. When the white hare heard, he set out to warn his master; in his absence the badger returned, killed the old woman, assumed her form, and converted her corpse into broth. 'I have made such excellent broth,' he told the returning husband, 'sit down and make a good meal!' The old man ate and pronounced it excellent — 'Excellent?' sneered the badger. 'You have eaten your wife! Her bones lie in that corner,' and he disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hare returned, grasped the situation, and scampered to the mountain resolved on vengeance. Creeping behind the badger, who carried a bundle of sticks, he set them alight so they crackled. 'What is this strange noise?' asked the badger. 'The Crackling Mountain,' replied the hare. The burning badger sprang into a river, but his scorched back was then treated by the delighted hare to a cayenne poultice. Later the hare invited the badger to sail to the moon in his boat; refusing, the badger built a boat of clay. Down the river went the wooden boat and the crumbling clay boat, and when the badger's vessel came to pieces the hare laughed derisively and killed his enemy with his oar. The loyal animal received much praise and loving care from his grateful master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Miraculous Tea-Kettle of Morinji

region.en: Morinji temple and a tinker's house (symbolic pin: Tatebayashi)
region.zh: 茂林寺與補鍋匠之家（象徵釘：館林）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A priest's old tea-kettle grows the head, tail and legs of a badger and dances wildly until boxed; sold to a tinker, it becomes a tight-rope-dancing fortune that draws princes and princesses and amasses riches, and is finally restored to Morinji temple to be worshipped as a precious treasure.
summary.zh: 僧人舊茶壺入火即長出狸之首尾四肢，飛舞於室；賣與補鍋匠後能歌舞走索，王侯爭看，匠人大富，最後將壺奉還茂林寺，供為寶物。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the bunbuku-chagama badger-kettle cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: A priest of Morinji temple set his old tea-kettle on the fire to make tea, and no sooner had it touched the fire than it changed into the head, tail and legs of a badger. The novices were called to see the sight: the badger with the body of a kettle rushed nimbly about the room, flew into the air and circled it again and again until the priests captured it and thrust it into a box. A tinker then called at the temple; the priest, thinking it a fine idea to sell his extraordinary kettle, bargained until the unsuspecting man bought it and took it away, assured he had done a good day's work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: That night the tinker was awakened by a sound close to his pillow: the kettle he had bought was not a kettle at all but a lively and clever badger. His friends advised him to take the animal on show, for it could dance and walk the tight-rope. The fame of the performing badger spread far and wide; princes and princesses came to see it, and from royal patronage and the delight of the people the tinker amassed a great fortune. When he had made his money he restored the kettle to Morinji temple, where it was worshipped as a precious treasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Vampire Cat and the Lady O Toyo

region.en: The Prince of Hizen's palace, Hizen province
region.zh: 肥前國諸侯宮邸

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A great cat strangles the favourite lady O Toyo, buries her, and takes her form; the Prince wastes nightly until the lowly soldier Ito Soda keeps a self-wounding vigil against the enchanted drowsiness, forces the cat to reveal itself, and the hunted beast is slain in the mountains.
summary.zh: 大貓扼死愛妾阿豐，埋屍於廊下，化其形貌。藩主夜夜衰弱，百名侍衛十時即睡。足輕伊藤守多忍痛以短刀刺股驅睡，兩夜逼退貓妖，並率八人搜殺；貓中箭遁走山中，終於狩獵中被誅。

sensitivity.note: Japanese vampire-cat legend of the Nabeshima clan cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Prince of Hizen lingered in the garden with O Toyo, the favourite among his ladies, unaware that a large cat followed them into the palace. At midnight O Toyo awoke to a dreadful presence: a gigantic cat crouched beside her, sprang upon her and strangled her. The animal made a hole under the verandah, buried the corpse, and assumed the form of the beautiful O Toyo. The Prince, unknowing, caressed a foul beast and grew dangerously ill, suffering most at night and troubled by horrible dreams; the hundred retainers set to watch him fell every night into a mysterious drowsiness at ten o'clock, and even three loyal councillors had the same experience.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: A priest named Ruiten, appointed to pray for the Prince, noticed a young soldier washing himself before an image of Buddha and praying for his lord's recovery. 'I am Ito Soda of the infantry of Nabeshima,' the man said, 'the Prince is bewitched, and if I might remain with him I would find and crush the evil power.' Admitted to the watch, Soda spread oil-paper on the mats and stuck his dirk into his thigh, twisting the knife as drowsiness returned; blood dripped steadily while the sliding doors opened and the false O Toyo crept in, smiled at the sleepers, and was always frustrated by the dauntless eyes of the watcher until she retired. The Prince at last slept peacefully and began to recover.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Soda planned to kill the creature in her own room, with eight retainers waiting outside. Posing as a messenger with a letter, he drew his dirk; the false O Toyo seized a halberd and blow answered blow until, seeing flight was better than battle, she threw away her weapon and in a moment the lovely maiden turned into a cat and sprang to the roof. The eight men shot at it but it escaped, made for the mountains and troubled the neighbourhood until it was killed during a hunt ordered by the Prince of Hizen. The Prince became well again, and Ito Soda received the honour and reward he so richly deserved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Man Who Made the Trees to Blossom
title.zh: 花咲爺——讓枯樹開花的老人

region.en: An old couple's cottage and a buried pine (symbolic pin: Edo region)
region.zh: 老夫婦茅屋與埋犬之松（象徵釘：江戶地方）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A faithful dog leads a kind old couple to buried treasure; killed by greedy neighbours, it returns as a spirit to guide its master to a magic mortar and its ashes that blossom withered trees — while the wicked neighbours, burning the mortar and scattering ashes in a prince's court, are beaten and driven off in disgrace.
summary.zh: 善良老翁的犬掘得金銀，被貪心鄰人借去又殺害埋於松下。犬靈指點：松木做臼舂米成寶；臼被惡鄰焚毀後，犬靈再教其以灰撒枯樹即開花。善翁受賞，惡鄰仿效卻使灰瞎了王子眼，遭痛打而逃。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the Hanasaka-jiisan cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old couple's dog became excited in the garden and sniffed one particular spot of ground; digging there, the old people unearthed gold and silver pieces and precious treasures, which they at once distributed in alms to the poor. The neighbours borrowed the dog and fed it delicacies, but the animal, previously ill-treated by them, refused to eat; where they dug at the sniffed spot they found only refuse. Angry and disappointed, they killed the dog and buried him under a pine-tree. The good old man, full of sorrow, laid food and flowers on the grave, weeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: That night the dog's spirit appeared and said: 'Cut down the tree where I am buried, and from the wood fashion a mortar, and think of me whenever you use it.' Rice ground in the pine mortar turned every grain to treasure. The wicked couple borrowed the mortar too, but for them the rice turned to filth, and in anger they broke and burnt the vessel. The dog's spirit came again: 'Sprinkle the ashes of the mortar over withered trees and they will immediately blossom.' Carrying a basket of ashes, the kind old man journeyed from village to town, and withered trees burst into flower; a prince commanded an exhibition and sent him home loaded with gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The neighbours gathered the remaining ashes and the greedy fellow went about claiming to revive dead trees. Summoned before the prince, he climbed into a tree and scattered the ashes, but the tree stayed withered and the flying ashes nearly blinded and suffocated the prince; the impostor was almost beaten to death and slunk away in misery. The kind old couple rebuked their neighbours for their wickedness, allowed them to share their wealth, and the once mean and crafty couple led good and virtuous lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jellyfish and the Monkey

region.en: Rin-Jin's palace beneath the sea; an island offshore (symbolic pin: Tango coast)
region.zh: 龍王海底宮殿與海上小島（象徵釘：丹後海岸）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The Dragon Queen will be cured only by a live monkey's liver; the jellyfish flatters a monkey into riding to the Dragon Palace, blunders out the true purpose, is outwitted by the tale of spare livers hanging on a pine, and returns empty — whereupon the enraged Sea King beats him until he loses his shell forever.
summary.zh: 龍后垂危，唯活猿之肝可救。水母奉命誘猿騎背入海，途中說漏真情；猿託詞松樹上掛著備用肝臟，騙水母載其回島，一躍而逃。龍王大怒，下令把水母打得骨頭不剩，水母從此失殼，子孫皆為軟體。

sensitivity.note: Japanese sea-king etiological folktale; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Rin-Jin, King of the Sea, had taken to wife a beautiful Dragon Princess, and when she fell ill no physician availed. 'If I eat the liver of a live monkey I shall recover,' sobbed the Queen. So Rin-Jin called the jellyfish and told him to swim to the land and return with a live monkey, telling him of the wonders of the deep — the palace with its floor of pearl and walls of coral. The jellyfish found a fine-looking monkey playing in a pine and sang the praises of the Kingdom of the Sea; the monkey accepted the invitation and seated himself comfortably on the thick shell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Halfway home the foolish jellyfish asked whether the monkey had brought his liver, and blurted out that a doctor would use it to save the sick Queen. The monkey lamented that he had forgotten it — 'I have several livers hanging up on a pine-tree; take me back to the island and I will fetch one.' The credulous jellyfish turned and swam back; the monkey sprang from his back and danced on the branches. 'Liver? You silly old jelly-fish, you'll certainly never get mine!' When the jellyfish told his dismal tale, the Sea King fell into a great passion: 'Beat him to a jelly! Beat this stupid fellow till he hasn't a bone left in his body!' So the jellyfish lost his shell from that hour, and all jellyfishes born after him remain nothing but jelly to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tongue-cut Sparrow

region.en: An old couple's cottage and the sparrow's home on a mountain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 老嫗洗衫處與雀居深山（象徵釘）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A cross neighbour cuts out a pet sparrow's tongue for eating her starch; the kindly owners find the bird feasting and dancing in his mountain home, and choose the light basket that proves an inexhaustible treasure — while the greedy tongue-cutter chooses the heavy basket and is torn to pieces by the devils inside.
summary.zh: 惡鄰老嫗誤雀食其漿糊，剪去雀舌。雀之主人翁媪入山尋雀，受雀家款待；臨別任選輕重二筐，老夫婦選輕筐，得金銀珠寶取之不竭；惡嫗貪選重筐，開之群鬼躍出將其撕碎。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the Shita-kiri Suzume cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: A cross old woman at her wash-tub found her neighbour's pet sparrow had eaten all the starch, mistaking it for food; in her anger she cut out the sparrow's tongue, and the bird flew away to a mountain. The old couple who owned the sparrow journeyed far until they found their pet again. Delighted, the sparrow begged them into his house, feasted them with fish and sake, had them waited upon by his wife, children and grandchildren, and danced for them the Sparrow's Dance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: When it was time to go home the sparrow brought out two wicker baskets, saying one was heavy and the other light, and asked which they would rather have. Choosing the light one for their age and the long journey, the old couple found on opening it gold, silver, jewels and silk — an inexhaustible supply that made them rich and prosperous. The cruel tongue-cutter hastened to the sparrow, chose the heavy basket hoping for more treasure, and when at last she opened it at home, devils sprang upon her and tore her to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Sanemori-San and the Cucumber Beetle

region.en: Rice-fields of Izumo
region.zh: 出雲稻田

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The warrior Sanemori, slain when his horse rolled in a rice-field, becomes the rice-devouring insect Sanemori-San, whom Izumo peasants summon each summer night with fires, flutes, gongs and a straw rider burnt or thrown into water; a guilty physician's angry ghost becomes the shiwan beetle that gnaws cucumbers.
summary.zh: 武者實盛因馬失蹄陷田而被殺，化為食稻之蟲「實盛蟲」。出雲農民夏夜於田中焚火、吹笛擊鑼，呼「實盛大人請來」，並焚或擲稻草騎者於水以驅蟲；又傳犯過的醫師被追殺，腳纏瓜藤而死，怨靈化為食瓜之蟲。

sensitivity.note: Japanese legends of humans transformed into insects, attached to living rites in Izumo; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Sanemori, a great warrior, was fighting on horseback when his horse slipped and rolled into a rice-field; his antagonist seized the chance to slay him, and from that hour Sanemori became a rice-devouring insect known to the peasantry of Izumo as Sanemori-San. On certain summer nights the peasants light fires in their rice-fields to attract the insect, play upon flutes and beat gongs, crying: 'O Sanemori, augustly deign to come hither!' A religious rite is performed, and a straw representation of a rider upon a horse is burnt or thrown into the water, which it is believed will free the fields from the rice-devouring insect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The shiwan, a small yellow insect that feeds upon cucumbers, is said to have once been a physician. This physician, guilty of some intrigue, was forced to leave his home; in attempting to escape his foot caught in the sinuous coils of a cucumber vine, and he was killed by his pursuers. His angry ghost became a shiwan, and from that day to this the insect feeds upon cucumbers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Daruma and the Legend of the Tea-Plant

region.en: Lo Yang, China, as retold in Japan (symbolic pin: Kyoto)
region.zh: 中國洛陽（日本傳述；象徵釘：京都）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The Indian sage Daruma, son of a Hindu king, meditates nine years facing the temptations of St Anthony until he falls asleep; in penance he cuts off his offending eyelids and casts them to the ground, where they become the first tea-plant — a drink that repels slumber for monks' vigils — and three years after death he walks the western mountains carrying one shoe.
summary.zh: 印度聖者達摩（禪宗初祖）面壁九年，因誦經入夢受魔誘；醒後大愧，自割雙瞼擲地，瞬即化為第一株茶樹，其葉能驅睡魔，供僧侶守夜之用。傳其死後三年有人見其行於中國西山，開棺僅得一履。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist etiological legend of Bodhidharma and the origin of tea; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Daruma was an Indian sage, said to have been the son of a Hindu king and to have received instruction from Panyatara. When his studies were complete he retired to Lo Yang and remained seated in meditation for nine years. During that period he was tempted after the manner of St Anthony; he wrestled against the temptations by reciting sacred scriptures, but the word 'jewel' lost its spiritual meaning and suggested the precious stone in a lovely woman's ear, and even 'lotus' suggested the opening of a girl's fair mouth. The temptation transported him to an Indian city, among strange deities, rajahs and dancing-girls, to a temple covered with foul forms, where it seemed he met and kissed the woman who had changed the meaning of jewel and lotus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddenly the vision departed and Daruma awoke under the Chinese sky, truly penitent for his neglect of devotions. Taking a knife from his girdle he cut off his eyelids and cast them upon the ground, saying: 'O Thou Perfectly Awakened!' The eyelids were transformed into the tea-plant, from whose leaves was made the beverage that repels slumber and allows good Buddhist priests their vigils. Daruma is generally shown without legs, for one version says he lost his limbs through the nine-year meditation; netsuke-carvers depict him scowling, with lidless eyes. Three years after his death he was seen walking across the western mountains of China carrying one shoe in his right hand; when his tomb was opened by order of the Emperor it contained only a shoe, which the saint had forgotten to take with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Hoichi-the-Earless

region.en: Amidaji temple and the cemetery of Akamagaseki, Dan-no-ura
region.zh: 赤間關阿彌陀寺與壇之浦墓園

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The blind biwa-player Hoichi is led nightly by a ghostly samurai to perform the Heike battles before a noble assembly — the Taira dead at their tombs — until his body is covered with sacred texts; the invisible visitor finds only two ears left uncovered and tears them off, and ever after he is called Hoichi-the-Earless.
summary.zh: 盲眼琵琶法師芳一每夜被幽靈武士引去，為平家亡靈誦唱壇之浦之戰。同伴以般若心經遍書其身，唯漏雙耳；夜來者遍尋不見其人，唯見雙耳，遂取以獻主。自此人稱「無耳芳一」。

sensitivity.note: Japanese ghost legend of the Taira dead, adapted from Lafcadio Hearn; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After the sea-fight of Dan-no-ura, where the Taira perished with their infant Emperor Antoku, the coast was haunted for seven hundred years by their ghosts; mysterious fires shone on the waves and the air was filled with the noise of warfare until the temple of Amidaji was built at Akamagaseki and a cemetery laid out around it. There lived a blind priest named Hoichi, famous for his recitation and his marvellous biwa-playing, above all for the story of the war between the Taira and Minamoto clans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: One warm evening a deep voice called 'Hoichi!' from the garden: his lord was staying at Akamagaseki with many noble followers and had heard how excellently the blind man recited the battle of Dan-no-ura. Led by a retainer with an iron grip, past a gate where 'Kaimon!' unbarred the doors, up steps and through rustling screens, Hoichi played to a vast assembly — the strings of his biwa imitating oars, ships, shouting men and whirring arrows — until, chanting of the women and children and of Niidono sinking a thousand fathoms with the infant Emperor in her arms, the company wept and wailed. Commanded to return nightly in secret, he did so; but his fellow priest grew suspicious, and the servants, following with lanterns, found him at the tomb of Antoku Tenno, playing and chanting loudly among mysterious fires like a gathering of lighted candles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Your great skill has called forth the ghosts of the Taira,' said the priest; 'you are in great danger.' He had an acolyte inscribe the sutra Hannya-Shin-Kyo upon every part of the blind man's body — breast, head, back, face, neck, arms, legs, even the soles of his feet — and bade him sit silent and still. That night the deep voice called and called, and the invisible visitor at last sprang onto the verandah: 'In place of the player I see only two ears! Those ears I will take to my lord!' Hoichi's ears were torn off, though he remained mute in agony, and thus the priest found him when he returned, with the trickling of blood on the verandah. 'It is all my fault — the acolyte failed to write the sacred texts on your ears.' From that day the blind priest was known as Mimi-nashi-Hoichi, Hoichi-the-Earless.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Corpse-Eater of Mino

region.en: A hermitage and hamlet in the province of Mino
region.zh: 美濃國草庵與村落

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: Lost in Mino, the priest Muso Kokushi is refused shelter by a churlish recluse but welcomed by a village where the corpse must be left alone; at night a terrible Shape devours the body and the offerings, and the rude hermit is unmasked as a jikininki — a greedy priest reborn as a man-eating goblin — whose hermitage then vanishes beside a moss-covered tomb.
summary.zh: 雪巷國師夜宿美濃山中草庵被拒，投宿村中恰逢喪事，眾人依俗離去，唯留僧守屍。夜半怪形現身食屍兼吞祭品。翌日村民言山上並無庵堂；僧再訪，老僧自認為食屍鬼（生前貪法衣之利而墮此報），言畢連庵俱滅，唯餘青苔古墓。

sensitivity.note: Japanese goblin legend adapted from Lafcadio Hearn; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Muso Kokushi, a priest, lost his way in the province of Mino and despaired of finding shelter till he came upon a little hermitage called anjitsu. The aged priest there greeted him churlishly: 'I never give shelter to any one. In yonder valley you will find a hamlet; seek a night's repose there.' At the headman's dwelling Muso was hospitably received, only to learn that the father of the house had died and that, by the custom of the village, all must go away at night because strange and terrible things happen to corpses when they are left alone — perhaps a priest would not be afraid to remain. Muso answered he was in no way afraid and performed the funeral service, keeping his solitary vigil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the night had far advanced a strange Shape advanced, so terrible that the priest could neither move nor speak. It raised the corpse and quickly devoured it; not content, it ate the offerings too, then vanished. In the morning the villagers returned and expressed no surprise that the corpse had disappeared; but when Muso mentioned the hermitage on the hill they were amazed — there was no priest and no anjitsu on yonder hill; he had been deluded by some evil spirit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Muso found the hermitage again, and the old priest came out bowing and ashamed: 'You have seen my real shape. I am a jikininki, a man-eating goblin. Many years ago I was a priest in this district and performed many burial services, but I was not influenced by true religion and thought only of the fine clothes I could get from my calling; for that reason I was reborn a jikininki and have ever since devoured the corpses of all who died here. Have pity on my miserable plight, and repeat certain prayers on my behalf, that I may speedily find peace.' The moment the words were spoken the recluse and his hermitage vanished, and Muso found himself kneeling beside a moss-covered tomb, probably the tomb of the unfortunate priest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Maiden with the Wooden Bowl

region.en: A rice-farming household (symbolic pin: Edo region)
region.zh: 稻作農家（象徵釘：江戶地方）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A dying mother fixes a lacquered bowl upon her beautiful daughter's head to hide her from temptation; hired as a servant, mocked by all, she refuses her master's son until her dead mother bids her in a dream — and at the wedding, as the bride raises the three-times-three cup, the bowl bursts with cries and groans and pours out gold, silver and jewels, revealing the most beautiful woman in all Japan.
summary.zh: 寡母恐女兒貌美招禍，臨終為她戴上木碗遮顏。姑娘入富農家為僕，受盡嘲弄；少主鍾情欲娶，她屢拒，直至亡母夢中囑婚。婚禮合巹之際，木碗呻吟碎裂，金銀珠寶傾瀉而出為嫁資，碗下竟是全日本最美的新娘。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the bowl-hidden bride cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old couple had one child, a girl of remarkable charm and beauty. When the father died the widow grew concerned for her daughter's future: 'Your face is all too fair. It must be hidden from the eager eyes of men, lest it cause you to fall from your good and simple life to one of shame.' She placed a lacquered bowl upon the maiden's head and bade her always wear it. Shortly after, the old woman died, and the maiden earned her living in the rice-fields, known throughout the country as the Maiden with the Bowl on her Head; young men laughed and tried to pull off the wooden covering, but it could not be removed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: A rich farmer, struck by her diligence, took her into his house to nurse his sick wife, and treated her as a child of their own. His eldest son, home from gay Kyoto, grew day by day more impressed by the girl's gentleness and nobility until he resolved to marry her; most of his relations opposed the union bitterly, and the maiden herself refused, believing marriage could only bring discord to the home that had sheltered her. That night her mother came to her in a dream: 'Marry the farmer's son and all will be well again.' She awoke full of joy and yielded with a gracious smile.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the wedding none could remove the bowl, which uttered strange cries and groans when the relations pulled at it. The bridegroom commanded the ceremony to proceed, and as the bride put the wine-cup to her lips for the three-times-three, the bowl broke with a great noise and from it fell gold and silver and precious stones, so the maiden who had been a beggar now had her marriage portion; and the guests, looking up, saw that the bride was the most beautiful woman in all Japan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Tokoyo and the Serpent God Yofune-Nushi

region.en: Rocky bay of the Oki Islands, and the sea cave of the serpent
region.zh: 隱岐群島岩灣與蛇神海底洞窟

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: Banished to the Oki Islands, Oribe Shima's daughter Tokoyo rows alone across the sea to find him; she saves a girl from sacrifice to the serpent god Yofune-Nushi, offers herself instead, dives with a dagger between her teeth into the cave where the white serpent guards a cursed image of Hojo Takatoki, blinds its right eye, pierces its heart, and by carrying the image ashore unwittingly cures the tyrant's disease and frees her father.
summary.zh: 織部島被流放隱岐，其女常世渡海尋父。夜聞少女將被獻祭蛇神夜船主，遂以身相代，口銜短劍潛入海底洞窟；洞中供著北條高時之像，白蛇瞪目竄出。常世先刺其右眼，再刺其心，斬之；抱神像與蛇屍出水。高時之疾恰在此時痊癒，織部島被赦還鄉，父女團聚。

sensitivity.note: Japanese hero-maiden legend adapted from R. Gordon Smith; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Oribe Shima had offended the great ruler Hojo Takatoki and was banished to Kamishima, one of the Oki Islands, forced to leave his beautiful daughter Tokoyo, whom he deeply loved. Unable to bear the separation, Tokoyo set out on a long journey to Akasaki in the province of Hoki; the fisher-folk laughed at her plan to row to the islands, but at nightfall she got into the lightest vessel she could find and by dint of a fair wind and persistent rowing came to one of the rocky bays of the Oki Islands. A fisherman warned her that the search might cost them both their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: That night, sleeping beneath a shrine dedicated to Buddha, Tokoyo was wakened by clapping of hands: a weeping maiden in white stood beside a priest who was about to push her over the rocks into the roaring sea. On the thirteenth of June, the priest explained, the Serpent God Yofune-Nushi demanded the sacrifice of a young girl, else he caused terrible storms. 'I am glad to have saved this poor girl's life,' said Tokoyo; 'I gladly offer myself in her place.' Taking the maiden's white robe and praying to the image of Buddha, she placed a small dagger between her teeth and plunged into the tempestuous sea, down through the moonlit water till she came to a mighty cave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the cave stood a statue of Hojo Takatoki, who had sent her father into exile; she was about to tie the image on her back when a great white serpent crept out with eyes gleaming angrily — Yofune-Nushi himself. Tokoyo drew her dagger and thrust it through the right eye; the serpent retired into the cave, she followed and struck at its heart, and with a shriek of pain it fell dead upon the cavern floor. The priest and the maiden on the rocks saw her rise to the surface carrying the image and a mighty fish-like creature. Reported to Hojo Takatoki, the story had a strange sequel: the ruler had long suffered from an incurable disease, and he regained his health precisely at the hour when his image — cursed and thrown into the sea by some exile — was restored. Hearing the brave girl was the daughter of the banished Oribe Shima, he sent her father home with all speed, where he and his daughter lived in peace and happiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kappa's Promise

region.en: The river Kawachi near Matsue, Izumo
region.zh: 出雲松江川內川

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The river goblin of the Kawachi drowns villagers and cattle until it seizes a horse and is dragged ashore and bound; refusing to write, the creature presses its inky hand upon a document swearing never to harm the village again, and the mark is still preserved in the temple of Kawako-no-miya — for to defeat a kappa is as unlucky as to be beaten by one.
summary.zh: 河童居川內川，屢害村民牲畜。一日擒馬失手，被拖上岸縛住。村人不忍殺之，令其立誓不害村中一人一畜；河童不能寫字，蘸墨按手印為據，放歸川中。其印至今存於川子神社，蓋河童不可殺亦不可勝——勝之者必衰。

sensitivity.note: Japanese river-goblin (kappa) legend of Izumo; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Kappa is a river goblin with the body of a tortoise and scaly limbs, an ape-like head with a cavity containing a mysterious fluid that is the source of its power. Fierce yet extremely polite, it challenges wayfarers to single combat, but a profound bow makes it bow in reply, spilling the strength-giving liquid from its cranium and rendering it feeble. To defeat the Kappa, however, is as unfortunate as to be beaten by it, for momentary glory is followed by a wasting away; in some parts of Japan it claims two victims every year, striking bathers in lake or river and sucking their blood like a vampire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In ancient days a Kappa dwelt in the river Kawachi and seized and destroyed villagers and their domestic animals. One day a horse entered the river and the Kappa, trying to capture it, twisted its neck; the frightened horse sprang up the bank into a neighbouring field with the Kappa still holding on, and the owner and many villagers securely bound the Child of the River. 'Let us kill this horrible creature,' said the peasants; but the owner answered: 'We will make him swear never to destroy the inhabitants or the domestic animals of this village.' A document was prepared and the Kappa was asked to sign it. 'I cannot write,' it replied, 'but I will dip my hand in ink and press it upon the document.' When the inky mark was made the creature was released to its river, and from that day to this the Kappa has remained true to its promise — the mark preserved in the little temple of Kawako-no-miya near Matsue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Yosho, the First Sennin of Japan

region.en: The mountains of Noto
region.zh: 能登山地

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: Born at Noto in 870 after his mother dreamt she swallowed the sun, the recluse Yosho lives on a single grain of millet a day and departs the earth in 901, leaving his mantle on a tree-branch bequeathed to Emmei of Dogen-ji; his stricken father, praying to see his son again, hears the Lotus of the Law recited overhead and is promised a monthly descent drawn by flowers and incense.
summary.zh: 能登聖人陽成，母夢吞日而生。日食一粟，誦法華經；901年離世，留衣缽於樹枝，遺書「以衣傳法眼寺榮明」。其父病篤思子，忽聞空中誦經——陽成言：每月十八日設花焚香，我魂必隨香降臨相見。

sensitivity.note: Japanese legend of the mountain-recluse sennin (Taoist-immortal cycle); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Sennin are mountain recluses who, though in human form, are immortal and adepts in the magical arts. The first great Japanese sennin was Yosho, born at Noto in A.D. 870; just before his birth his mother dreamt she had swallowed the sun, a dream that foretold the miraculous power of her child. Studious and devout, Yosho spent most of his time studying the 'Lotus of the Law', lived very simply, and at length reduced his diet to a single grain of millet a day. He departed from the earth in A.D. 901, having attained much supernatural power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yosho left his mantle hanging on the branch of a tree, together with a scroll bearing the words: 'I bequeath my mantle to Emmei of Dogen-ji.' In due time Emmei became a sennin and, like his master, performed many marvels. Shortly after Yosho's disappearance his father became seriously ill and prayed ardently to see his well-loved son again; in reply Yosho's voice was heard overhead reciting the 'Lotus of the Law', and when the recitation ended he said to his stricken father: 'If flowers are offered and incense burned on the 18th of every month, my spirit will descend and greet you, drawn by the perfume of the flowers and the blue smoke of incense.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Shojo's White Sake

region.en: The seashore below the miraculous Mount Fuji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 富士山麓海濱（象徵釘）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A dying father's wish for sake sends the boy Koyuri to the shore, where red-haired sea-monsters fill his gourd with their sacred white sake that restores youth to the good; a jealous neighbour who beats the boy tastes only filthy water and is poisoned until he repents — then Yurine and Mamikiko brew the Shojo's sake on Fuji's southern side and live three hundred years.
summary.zh: 油根病危思酒，其子小百合海濱遇紅髮海妖，以葫芦乞得白酒，父飲之病癒。貪鄰萬吉仗勢索酒，入口即吐，反而毒發；海妖自稱猩猩，白酒可使善者延年、貪者中毒。服藥悔過後得赦；後二人於富士南麓釀猩猩酒，活三百歲。

sensitivity.note: Japanese sea-monster (shojo) legend adapted from R. Gordon Smith; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: On the day following the miraculous appearance of Mount Fuji a poor man named Yurine, who lived near the mountain, became extremely ill and desired to drink a cup of sake before he died. But there was no rice wine in the hut, and his boy Koyuri wandered along the shore with a gourd in his hand. There he found two strange creatures with long red hair and skin the colour of pink cherry-blossom, wearing green seaweed girdles, drinking white sake from large flat cups replenished from a great stone jar. 'My father is dying and much desires a cup of sake,' said the boy; and one of the creatures filled his gourd. The old man drank eagerly: 'This is no common wine. It has given me strength, and already I feel new life flowing through my old veins.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yurine's neighbour Mamikiko, hearing of the supply, grew jealous, snatched the gourd, spat out the sake as filthy water and beat the boy, forcing him to lead the way to the red-haired people. Koyuri wept as he told how his honesty had been doubted; the red man refilled the gourd and chuckled over Mamikiko's experience, then filled his huge cup — and the greedy man felt sick at the first taste. 'You are not aware that I am a Shojo and live near the Sea Dragon's Palace. This sacred white sake restores youth and years to human beings, and to Shojo it vanquishes death; to the greedy and selfish it is poison.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Poison?' groaned the contrite Mamikiko; 'good Shojo, have mercy and spare my life!' The Shojo gave him a powder, saying: 'Swallow this in sake and repent of your wickedness.' He did so, and this time the white sake was delicious. Mamikiko lost no time in making friends with Yurine, and some years later the two men took up their abode on the southern side of Mount Fuji, brewed the Shojo's white sake, and lived for three hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Issunboshi and the Magic Mallet

region.en: The Prince Sanjo's house and the Temple of Kwannon, Kyoto
region.zh: 三條殿與觀音堂（京都）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: An old couple who pray to the deified Empress Jingo for a child 'even if no bigger than a finger' receive exactly that, and angrily send the One-Inch Priest away; sailing a soup-bowl with a chopstick to Kyoto, he becomes the Princess Sanjo's page, defeats two oni from inside the first one's stomach, and when the Princess taps the oni's dropped lucky mallet, his wish to be as big as other people is granted — ending as a great lord married to the Princess.
summary.zh: 老夫婦向神功皇后神社求子：「小如指頭也好。」果然得一寸法師，十三歲不長，遂辭親出遊。以湯碗為舟、筷子為槳，抵京都為三條公主侍童。參拜觀音堂時二鬼攔路，一鬼吞之，一寸法師於鬼腹中持針劍亂刺，鬼咳而吐出；再登另一鬼鼻孔刺其目，二鬼逃遁。公主拾鬼遺小槌擊地祝禱，一寸法師頃刻長成正常青年，終成大官，娶三條氏幼女。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the Issunboshi cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old married couple went to the shrine of the deified Empress Jingo and prayed that they might be blessed with a child, even if it were no bigger than one of their fingers. A voice sounded from behind the bamboo curtain, and they were told their wish would be granted. In due time the old woman gave birth to a child no bigger than a little finger; the parents were extremely angry, though the Empress had fulfilled their prayer to the letter. The little fellow was called Issunboshi, the One-Inch Priest, and at thirteen he was still the same size as at birth, so exasperated were his parents at neighbours' jeers — 'Little Finger', 'Grain-of-Corn' — that they determined to send him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: He asked for a needle, a small soup-bowl and a chop-stick, and set off on his adventures, propelling the bowl like a boat with the chop-stick until he reached Kyoto. At the house of Prince Sanjo his minute voice won him a place, and he became the Princess Sanjo's page, accompanying his mistress everywhere. One day, leaving the Temple of Kwannon, two oni (evil spirits) sprang upon them. Issunboshi drew his needle-sword from its hollow straw; one oni laughed, 'I could swallow you as a cormorant swallows a trout, my funny little bean-seed, and I will!' — and opened its mouth, and the little hero found himself slipping down a huge dark throat. Nothing daunted, he bored away with his needle-sword until the spirit coughed him back into the sunny world; the second oni fared worse, for Issunboshi climbed its nostril and pierced its eyes, and both creatures fled yelling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way home the Princess picked up a small wooden mallet dropped by the wicked oni — a lucky mallet: 'You have only to wish and then tap it upon the ground, and your wish, no matter what, is always granted.' When Issunboshi wished to be as big as other people, the Princess tapped the mallet on the ground and in a moment he was transformed from a bijou creature to a lad just like other youths of his age. The curious Emperor summoned him, gave him many gifts and made him a high official; finally Issunboshi became a great lord and married Prince Sanjo's youngest daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Kintaro, the Golden Boy of Ashigara
title.zh: 金太郎——足柄山黃金童子

region.en: Ashigara Mountain
region.zh: 足柄山

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: Born to the disgraced courtier Sakata Kurando and the lady Yaegiri on lonely Ashigara Mountain, the Golden Boy fells trees like a woodcutter and speaks the language of bear, deer, hare and monkey; he uproots a tree to bridge a river before the astounded hero Yorimitsu, who takes the boy as retainer, names him Sakata Kintoki, and makes him a famous warrior whom children still carry in their bosoms.
summary.zh: 禁軍武士坂田藏人不名誉離京，與女嬖八重切逃亡成婚未果而自盡。八重切於足柄山生金太郎：孩提持斧伐木如樵，與熊鹿猿兔為友，通獸語。一日拔樹為橋渡溪，適為賴光所見，遣人問明來歷，收其為家臣，賜名坂田金時，後成名武將，孩童至今佩其像。

sensitivity.note: Japanese hero-legend of Kintaro/Sakata Kintoki; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Sakata Kurando, an officer of the Emperor's bodyguard, brave yet gentle, loved the beautiful lady Yaegiri; falling into disgrace, he left the Court to become a travelling tobacco merchant. Yaegiri escaped her home and wandered the country until she found him — but the unhappy man put an end to his humiliation by taking his own life. When she had buried her lover she went to Ashigara Mountain, where she gave birth to a child called Kintaro, the Golden Boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kintaro was remarkable for extreme strength: when only a few years old his mother gave him an axe with which he felled trees as quickly as an experienced woodcutter. Lonely on the desolate mountain, he made companions of the bear, deer, hare and monkey and spoke their strange language. One day he arranged a wrestling match, a kindly old bear digging the daïs, a hare and a monkey grappling while a deer gave encouragement and kept the sport fair; Kintaro tactfully rewarded the equally strong pair with tempting rice-cakes. Coming to a river on the way home, he put his strong arms round a tree on the bank and pulled it across so that it formed a bridge — and the famous hero Yorimitsu and his retainers witnessed the extraordinary feat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Watanabe Isuna followed Kintaro home and learned his story from Yaegiri. Yorimitsu came himself: 'If you will give me your child I will make him my retainer.' The woman gladly consented, and the Golden Boy went away with the great hero, who named him Sakata Kintoki. He became a famous warrior whose wonderful deeds are recited to this day, and children regard him as their favourite hero; little boys who would emulate his strength and bravery carry his portrait in their bosoms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Old Man Lost His Wen

region.en: A hollow tree in the mountains (symbolic pin: Edo region)
region.zh: 山中空心樹（象徵釘：江戶地方）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: An old wood-cutter shelters from a storm in a hollow tree where demons dance; his unexpected good dancing delights them, and their chief removes the wen from his cheek as a pledge for tomorrow's performance — while the wicked neighbour who next hides in the tree dances so badly that the demons fling the wen back onto his right cheek, leaving him a wen on either side.
summary.zh: 老翁避雨躲進空心樹，窺見群鬼宴舞。鬼王嫌其舞伴笨拙，老翁不自覺失笑而現身獻舞；群鬼大喜，邀翌夜再舞，並以他右頰之瘤為質，無痛取下。惡鄰仿效前來，舞藝低劣惹鬼厭，臨走把昨夜質物——那顆瘤——擲回他右頰；從此惡鄰左右各一瘤。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the Kobu-tori Jii cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: There was once an old man who had a wen on his right cheek that all medicines had made worse. One night, returning home laden with firewood, he was overtaken by a terrible thunderstorm and sheltered in a hollow tree. When the storm abated he heard sounds of merriment close at hand: a number of demons dancing, singing and drinking, one dancing clumsily by himself while the chief of the company was none too pleased. Forgetting caution, the old man left the tree, and when the leader cried, 'Enough! Is there no one who can dance better than this fellow?' it seemed that his youth returned; having once been an expert dancer, he offered to show his skill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXXI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The demons congratulated the old man on his performance, offered him a cup of sake and begged for more dances. When he agreed to dance again the following night, the chief said he must leave a pledge behind — and seeing the wen on the right cheek, judged it an excellent one, removing it without inflicting any pain before he and his companions vanished. The old man could scarcely realise that after many years of disfigurement he had at last lost his troublesome wen, and his old wife was none the less pleased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXXI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: A wicked and cantankerous neighbour, afflicted for many years with a wen on his left cheek, heard the story and hid in the hollow tree at sunset. Before long one of the company said: 'The old man is a long time coming. I made sure he would keep his promise.' At these words the fellow crept out, flourished his fan and began to dance — but he knew nothing of dancing, and his extraordinary antics displeased the demons greatly. 'You dance extremely ill, and the sooner you stop the better we shall be pleased; but before you depart we will return the pledge you left with us last night.' The demon flung the wen at the right cheek of the old man, where it remained firmly fixed; so the deceiver went away with a wen on either side of his face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXXI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fox-Bride and the Garden Shrine

region.en: The Inari shrines and fox-gardens of Kyoto: Mount Fushime and the miniature-mountain shrine garden
region.zh: 京都稻荷神社與庭園狐塚（伏見稻荷山）

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The bad fox's chief attribute is to delude human beings by taking the form of a beautiful woman — a shadow on water shows only the fox, a dog's glance strips the disguise — and the fullest fox-bride story in Davis is the Jewel Maiden, a fox who took bride-form at an emperor's court and was traced, life after life, back to the fox; at the garden shrine of the fox-god Inari the same creature-power is domesticated as stone foxes, and the household fox-ghost of the garden mountain watches over the people the god swore with Kobo Daishi to protect.
summary.zh: 惡狐最善化身美婦惑人：影落水中現狐形，遇犬則現原身。 Davis 書中最完整的「狐新娘」故事即「玉面夫人」——狐女入宮為妃，害主敗露，化狐而逃，歷劫受戒；而稻荷神社庭園中的石狐，則是同一神力的家宅化：與弘法大師立誓「你我一齊守護此民」的稻荷，以狐使的形式守在每一戶庭園的神龕旁。

sensitivity.note: Fox-woman (kitsune) legend cycle from Davis ch. V/XIX, central to living Japanese Inari worship; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text, presented for comparative mythology. The fox-bride episode-complex is conserved here with cross-references to the sibling base records rather than re-cut as duplicate episodes.

passages.text: All foxes possess supernatural powers to an almost limitless degree, and the chief attribute of the bad fox is the power to delude human beings by taking the form of a beautiful woman — the fox-bride — of whom many legends are told. Two tests reveal her: if the shadow of a fox-woman chance to fall upon water, only the fox, and not the fair woman, is revealed; and if a dog sees a fox-woman, the feminine form vanishes immediately and the fox alone remains. Demoniacal possession is frequently ascribed to foxes — kitsune-tsuki — the sufferer usually a sensitive woman of the poorer classes, into whose breast or finger-nails the fox enters, living a separate life of its own and speaking in a voice totally different from the human.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fullest fox-bride story is that of the fox who became the Jewel Maiden, concubine to the Emperor at the court of the Rising Sun. At a great feast in the Summer Palace, black clouds raced across a starless sky and a mysterious wind blew out every lantern; from the Jewel Maiden's frame there darted a weirdly lustrous flame that filled the imperial halls, and from that hour the Mikado sickened until the Court Magician declared that she was a fiend who, with insidious art, ravaged the State by captivating the Emperor's heart. Spurned, the sorceress resumed her original shape, that of a fox, and ran away pursued by dogs and arrows until she sank exhausted into the Death-Stone on Nasu moor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the priest Genno offered flowers, incense and scripture before the Death-Stone, the spirit within confessed her former lives: a demon honoured by a prince in Ind, the consort of an emperor in Great Cathay, and at last the fox-bride of Japan; reborn to virtue by the priest's intercession, she swore an oath firm as the Death-Stone that from that hour she was virtue's child alone. On its beneficent side the same fox power stands at the garden shrines: Inari, the fox-god, appeared to Kobo Daishi on Mount Fushime, accepted his sacrifice, and heard the saint say, 'Together, you and I, we will protect this people'; stone foxes wag their tails at a woman's prayer for a child, and when the mean rich man Raiko struck at his nightly visitor with a dagger, the trail of blood-spots led through the garden to a miniature mountain where a great creature begged the servants to persuade their master not to attack the Gods nor to be mean again — Inari, who had taken beast-shape to teach the old man a lesson.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V and ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
In Japan the fox is the great shape-shifter of legend, and its power for good or evil stands under the fox-god Inari, originally the God of Rice, who in the eleventh century became identified with the Fox God. All foxes possess supernatural powers to an almost limitless degree: infinite vision, the hearing of every secret thought of humankind, and above all the power of transformation. The chief attribute of the bad fox is the power to delude human beings, and for this purpose it will take the form of a beautiful woman — the fox-bride — and many are the legends told in this connection. Two tests expose her. If the shadow of a fox-woman chance to fall upon water, only the fox, and not the fair woman, is revealed; and if a dog sees a fox-woman, the feminine form vanishes immediately and the fox alone remains. Demoniacal possession is frequently ascribed to the evil influence of foxes — kitsune-tsuki — the sufferer usually a sensitive woman of the poorer classes into whose breast or finger-nails the fox enters, living a separate life of its own and speaking in a voice totally different from the human.

The fullest fox-bride narrative Davis retells is the Death-Stone legend, whose heroine is the fox that became the Jewel Maiden, Flawless Jewel, concubine to the Emperor Toba at the court of the Rising Sun. At a great feast in the Summer Palace, while the wit, wisdom and beauty of the land ate and drank to music, black clouds raced across a starless sky and a mysterious wind blew out every lantern; and from the Jewel Maiden's frame there darted a weirdly lustrous flame that filled the imperial halls. From that hour the Mikado sickened, until the Court Magician declared that the Jewel Maiden was a fiend who, with insidious art, ravaged the State by captivating the Emperor's heart. Spurned, the sorceress resumed her original shape, that of a fox, and fled to the Death-Stone on Nasu moor — pursued by dogs and arrows, sinking exhausted into the stone, from time to time haunting the moor until the priest Genno, offering flowers, incense and scripture, conjured her to confess her former lives: a demon honoured by a prince in Ind, the consort of an emperor in Great Cathay, and at last the fox-bride of Japan. Reborn to virtue by the priest's intercession, she swore an oath firm as the Death-Stone that from that hour she was virtue's child alone. The fox-bride, in other words, is a coming and vanishing creature of alluring but destructive power — a Japanese version, Davis says, of Fata Morgana.

The fox-garden shrine shows the other face of the same animal power. When Kobo Daishi returned from China, holy and wonder-working, Inari appeared to him on Mount Fushime and accepted the sacrifice he offered, and the saint said: 'Together, you and I, we will protect this people.' From that compact the fox-god became the guardian of households: beneficent Inari cures coughs and colds, brings wealth to the needy, and answers a woman's prayer for a child — though only a part of the reward is real, for at least one tempting coin is bound to turn quickly into grass, and the little good done by Inari is weighed down by countless mischiefs of his fox-children. At the garden shrines the foxes stand in stone, and once, when the mean rich man Raiko was drained of life-blood by a nightly priest-visitor and struck out with his dagger in the dark, the trail of blood-spots led his servants through the garden to a miniature mountain at the extreme end, where from a large hole protruded the upper part of an enormous spider that begged them to persuade their master not to attack the Gods nor to be mean again — Inari, who had assumed the shape of priest and beast to teach the old man a lesson. The fox-bride of the court and the stone foxes of the garden are one continuous power: the deluding woman-form that enters human houses as bride and bedevils them, and the fox at the shrine that enters the same houses as protector, teacher and trickster, watching over the people Inari swore with Kobo Daishi to protect.
narrative.zh: 狐狸是日本傳說中最大的變形者，其善惡之力皆繫於稻荷神（原為米神，十一世紀起與狐神同體）。狐能無限視聽、知人心念，尤擅變化；惡狐最善化身美婦惑人——即「狐新娘」。影子落水現狐形、遇犬現原身，是識破二法。狐憑（kitsune-tsuki）多附敏感貧婦，自乳間或指縫入體，別有聲口。玉面夫人即狐新娘之最著者：宮中惑主，宴上現妖光，被魔師道破，化狐逃至那須野殺生石，被犬矢追逼，力竭入石；經Genno上人供花焚香誦經，方自陳前世——天竺王侯所敬之魔、震旦岩皇帝妃（Hoji）、日本帝妃玉面夫人——遂誓向善。狐園神社則見同一神力之善面：弘法大師歸國後，稻荷於伏見山受其供養，大師言「你我一齊守護此民」；自此稻荷以石狐守家宅，治病賜財、應婦人求子之禱（然所賜錢必有一枚化草）；慳吝的賴光被夜半「法師」吸血，拔刀亂揮，血點引家人至園中假山，石縫中巨蜘蛛（稻荷所化）勸其勿犯神明、勿再慳吝。狐新娘與園中石狐，一為入戶惑人的婦形，一為守戶教人的獸形，同是稻荷狐狸之力。

functions: Explains and polices the boundary between human marriage and animal otherworld: the fox-bride motif warns households against marriages and seductions whose origin cannot be traced.
Provides the diagnostic tests (shadow on water, dog's revelation) that structure fox-woman detection tales across Japanese folklore and into modern fiction.

Domesticates the same dangerous power at the Inari shrine: the fox as household guardian and rice-god's messenger, binding field fertility, prosperity and child-giving to the compact of Kobo Daishi and Inari.
Frames kitsune-tsuki (fox possession) as an interpretive category for trance, illness and spirit speech in folk healing.
